title: Backend track (ขอบคุณครับ claude)
subtitle: Zero to contributing on a production Go service. Nine tiers, in order — each assumes the last is finished.

target.heading: What this is aimed at
target.body: A project with live Go API. Nothing here is filler — every tier maps to something that service does.

tiers.name: Ground floor
tiers.goal: Command line, Git, and enough JavaScript to stop guessing.
tiers.proof: You can create a repo, make three commits, and push it without looking anything up.

tasks.text: Navigate, move and delete files from the terminal
Install Node and run a .js file from the command line
Install a package with npm
git init, add, commit, push to a remote you created
Branch, change, merge back
Values, functions, arrays, objects, loops
map, filter, find, reduce
JSON and how to parse it
Callbacks, promises, async/await
Explain why await inside forEach does not work

tiers.name: First server
tiers.goal: How the web talks, and a server you wrote answering it.
tiers.proof: Four endpoints you can hit from the browser and from curl.

tasks.text: GET, POST, PATCH, PUT, DELETE and what each means
Status codes you'll actually use
Headers and bodies — inspect a real request
What stateless means and why it matters
Serve GET /hello returning JSON
POST that accepts a body and echoes it
A route with a URL parameter
Correct status codes for bad input
Hit every endpoint with curl, not just the browser

tiers.name: Typed and structured
tiers.goal: TypeScript, and code split into layers instead of one long file.
tiers.proof: No route handler longer than fifteen lines, and logic lives outside the handler.

tasks.text: tsconfig and a working build
Type annotations, interfaces, unions, optional fields
Generics — enough to read them, not to write them
Read a signature you didn't write and know what it wants
Type every request and response
Split routes, logic, and data access
Validate input and reject it properly
One consistent error shape
Config from environment, never in code

tiers.name: Real data
tiers.goal: Design a data model, then PostgreSQL, SQL by hand, and schema changes under version control.
tiers.proof: A schema you designed and can defend, a join you wrote unaided, and a balance two simultaneous requests cannot double-spend.

tasks.text: Take a real system and list its entities before writing any SQL
Decide what is a table, what is a column, what is a relationship
Normalize it, then say out loud where you'd denormalize and why
Choose primary keys and defend serial vs uuid for this case
Design the API resources over that schema — paths, methods, shapes
Write down three decisions you made and the alternative you rejected
Install Postgres and connect with psql
CREATE TABLE with real types and constraints
INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE by hand
WHERE, ORDER BY, LIMIT, GROUP BY
Foreign keys and one-to-many
Inner and left joins, and when you need which
Indexes and when to add one
Transactions, and rolling back when step two fails
What happens when two requests read the same row
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE and what it costs
Optimistic concurrency with version columns
Isolation levels and when they matter
Migrations in version control
Replace all in-memory data with Postgres

tiers.name: Who are you
tiers.goal: Authentication, authorization, and the gap between them.
tiers.proof: Two users log in and neither can read or modify the other's data.

tasks.text: Hash passwords with bcrypt or argon2
Issue a JWT and verify it
Access tokens vs refresh tokens
Middleware rejecting unauthenticated requests
Check the caller owns what they're touching
Roles, and admin-only routes
Try to break your own auth with someone else's ID
OAuth2 authorization code flow and PKCE
OIDC: ID tokens and how SSO works
Log into a dummy app with a real provider
Redirect allowlisting
Keep tokens server-side, not in the browser

tiers.name: Shipped
tiers.goal: It runs on someone else's machine, and tests gate the merge.
tiers.proof: A stranger clones the repo, runs one command, and has it working.

tasks.text: A Dockerfile for your API
compose bringing up API and Postgres together
Images vs containers vs volumes
Tests for your business logic
CI running lint and tests on every push
Deployed at a real URL
A README explaining setup and decisions

tiers.name: Go
tiers.goal: A second language, chosen because the target is written in it.
tiers.proof: You can read unfamiliar Go and say what it does.

tasks.text: A Tour of Go, all of it
Structs, methods, pointers
Interfaces — implicit, and why that changes design
Errors as values, not exceptions
Goroutines and channels, basics only
Packages, modules, go.mod
Write and run a test
Rewrite /hello in Go

tiers.name: A service, properly built
tiers.goal: Everything above, in Go, structured the way the target is.
tiers.proof: Layered, migrated, containerized, deployed — and your business logic does not import your web framework.

tasks.text: Route with Fiber or Gin
handler → usecase → repository, no shortcuts
Each layer's contract as an interface
Ports and adapters: name it, then see it in your own code
Constructor injection, never construct inside
cmd/ and internal/ layout
A mock repository injected into a usecase test
Table-driven tests for business rules
Tests that pass with no database running
Swap one adapter without touching a usecase
An ORM talking to Postgres
Migrations under version control
A multi-step write that cannot half-complete
JWT auth with real ownership checks
Structured logging, not fmt.Println
Generated API docs
Dockerfile, compose, CI, deployed
Redis for something that genuinely benefits from caching
Load test with vegeta, record before and after
Add an index because a load test told you to

tiers.name: The target
tiers.goal: Read the service and be able to contribute to it.
tiers.proof: You can trace any endpoint end to end and open a pull request that would survive review.

tasks.text: Clone it and get it running locally
Trace one endpoint from route to database
List everything unfamiliar, then work through the list
Map its domain layout against your layer layout
Read its interfaces and how they're injected at startup
Find every transaction and say what breaks without it
Find the Redis usage and explain why it's there
Read its auth middleware against yours
Follow its OAuth login including the redirect checks
Read its CI and deploy config end to end
Read merged PRs to learn what reviewers ask for
Find a real bug, rough edge, or missing test
Open a pull request
